# Computational fluid dynamics

---

## Computational fluid dynamics

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- We have now covered all the major algorithms for the class. Onto topics in physics!
- First up: computational fluid dynamics.
  - Many particles together acting under conservation of mass and momentum
  - Simple cases are incompressible fluids without friction
    - “Newtonian fluids”
  - Governed by the Navier–Stokes equations.
- References:
  - CFDPython by Prof. Lorena Barba:
    - Jupyter lessons on [github](https://github.com/barbagroup/CFDPython/tree/master/lessons)
    - Lectures on [youtube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SrIf-A7kc0Y&list=PL30F4C5ABCE62CB61)
  - [https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter30.pdf](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter30.pdf)

## Mass conservation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Consider a volume ($V$) inside a fluid.
  - Could be a small box ($dxdydz$), could be anything.
- Fluid velocity: $\vec{u}$
- Mass ($m$) inside $V$: integral of the density ($ \rho $),
  - $$m= \int  \rho dV$$
- Our first equation is just mass conservation: change in mass given by fluid flow at surfaces.
  - In differential form (i.e. use divergence theorem):

![](../assets/7.0_advdiffeq/slide05_pasted-movie.png){fig-alt="TODO"}

- Differential volume in a fluid
- $$\frac{dm}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt} \int  \rho dV=- \int d\vec{S} \cdot  \rho \vec{u}$$

- $$\frac{ \partial  \rho }{ \partial t}+\vec{ \nabla } \cdot  \rho \vec{u}=0$$

---

## Momentum conservation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- The other equations come from Newton's 2nd law (conservation of momentum):
  - Consider the motion of our small cube. Newton's 2nd law gives:
    - $$ \rho \frac{d\vec{u}}{dt}=\vec{F}$$
  - But the cube is moving (it's position depends on time), so we need to apply the chain rule. The full time derivative is:

- $$\frac{d\vec{u}}{dt}=\frac{ \partial \vec{u}}{ \partial t}+(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{ \nabla })\vec{u}=\vec{F}$$

- Change in fluid velocity
- at a fixed point in space

- Change in fluid velocity due to motion of fluid from neighboring points (advection)

---

## Momentum conservation

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Different types of forces to consider:
  - "Body forces" acting on the whole system, e.g. gravity ($\vec{F}=\vec{g}$)
  - "Surface forces" (divide into normal and tangential/shear stresses)
    - Dynamic viscosity coefficient ($ \mu $)
    - Bulk viscosity coefficient ($ \xi $)
    - Pressure ($p$)
- The total force is:
  - This contains forces due to pressure and friction.
  - (For derivation, see [Barba's lectures](https://youtu.be/7UpOXp_i4cc?si=TpZImGYCLZ4d6CTp))

- $$\vec{F}= \mu { \nabla }^{2}\vec{u}+( \mu + \xi )\vec{ \nabla }(\vec{ \nabla } \cdot \vec{u})+\vec{g}$$

![Screenshot 2026-02-02 at 11.35.48 AM.png](../assets/7.0_advdiffeq/Screenshot-2026-02-02-at-11.35.48-AM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}

- Forces acting on a differential fluid surface

---

## Momentum conservation

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- For an incompressible, Newtonian fluid:
  - $$\vec{ \nabla } \cdot \vec{u}=0$$
  - Stresses proportional to velocity gradient
- ...we get the Navier–Stokes equations
  - (with $ \nu  \equiv  \mu / \rho $):

- $$\frac{ \partial \vec{u}}{ \partial t}+(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{ \nabla })\vec{u}=\vec{g}-\frac{1}{ \rho }\vec{ \nabla }p+ \nu { \nabla }^{2}\vec{u}$$

---

## 1D Navier–Stokes

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- In 1D, we have:

- $$\frac{ \partial u}{ \partial t}+u\frac{ \partial u}{ \partial x}=g-\frac{1}{ \rho }\frac{ \partial p}{ \partial t}+ \nu \frac{{ \partial }^{2}u}{ \partial {x}^{2}}$$

- If $g=0$ and $\frac{dp}{dt}=0$, we get Burger's equation from last semester:

- $$\frac{ \partial u}{ \partial t}+u\frac{ \partial u}{ \partial x}= \nu \frac{{ \partial }^{2}u}{ \partial {x}^{2}}$$

- So, Navier–Stokes describes shock propagation.

---

## ND Navier–Stokes

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- What about solutions in N dimensions?
  - This is a million dollar question! [https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)
  - [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness)
- So, numerical solutions are often the only way to go.

# General relativity

---

## General relativity

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- A similar problem (computationally speaking): general relativity.
  - It's also an extremely difficult problem: analytical solutions are hard to come by, so numerical methods are essential.
- GR relates gravity to the curvature of spacetime:

- Objects with mass or energy distort space-time, and this induces a gravitational field.

- arXiv:astro-ph/9901124

![Spacetime_curvature.tiff](../assets/7.0_advdiffeq/Spacetime_curvature.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}

- Cartoon of spacetime distortion

## General relativity

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- arXiv:astro-ph/9901124

- Space-time is a tensor.
- So gravity is a tensor.
- Einstein’s equations :

- $${G}_{ \mu  \nu }={R}_{ \mu  \nu }-\frac{1}{2}{g}_{ \mu  \nu }R=\frac{8 \pi {G}_{N}}{{c}^{4}}{T}_{ \mu  \nu }-{g}_{ \mu  \nu } \Lambda $$

- Ricci tensor
- (gravitational force)

- Metric tensor

- Curvature scalar

- Newton's constant

- Speed of light

- Stress-energy tensor
- (energy and momentum density of matter + radiation)

- Cosmological constant

- Huge set of nonlinear partial differential equations.
- Arbitrarily complicated (${T}_{ \mu  \nu }$ can be anything!)

- Einstein tensor

- Repeat from lectures on fitting

## Cosmological solutions to Einstein's equations

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- A few simple cases can be derived.
- If spacetime is homogeneous and isotropic, this is the Robertson–Walker metric:

- $$d{s}^{2}=\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{ \mu =0}}\limits^{3}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{ \nu =0}}\limits^{3}{g}_{ \mu  \nu }d{x}^{ \mu }d{x}^{ \nu }={c}^{2}d{t}^{2}-{R}^{2}(t)\left[ \frac{d{r}^{2}}{1-k{r}^{2}}+{r}^{2}(d{ \theta }^{2}+si{n}^{2} \theta d{ \phi }^{2})right] \right]$$

- R(t) = "cosmological scale factor"

- Friedmann–Lamaitre equations: assume that matter and radiation behave like a uniform, perfect fluid with density $ \rho $ and pressure $p$.

- $$\begin{matrix}
{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=\frac{8 \pi {G}_{N} \rho }{3}-\frac{k{c}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}+\frac{ \Lambda {c}^{2}}{3} \\
\frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}{R} & =-\frac{4 \pi {G}_{N}}{3}( \rho +3p)+\frac{ \Lambda {c}^{2}}{3}
\end{matrix}$$

- Repeat from lectures on fitting

- Hubble parameter : H(t0) = 72 km/s/Mpc  at present time

## Friedmann–Lemaître equations

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- A closer look at our PDE problem:

- $$\begin{matrix}
{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=\frac{8 \pi {G}_{N} \rho }{3}-\frac{k{c}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}+\frac{ \Lambda {c}^{2}}{3} \\
\frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}{R} & =-\frac{4 \pi {G}_{N}}{3}( \rho +3p)+\frac{ \Lambda {c}^{2}}{3}
\end{matrix}$$

- Hubble parameter $H(t)$
- At present, $H({t}_{0})=72$ km/s/MPc

- $ \rho (t)=$density

- Constants

- $R(t)=$cosmological scale factor

- $p=$pressure

- Value of $k$:
  - $k=1$: closed 3-sphere
  - $k=0$: flat
  - $k=-1$: open 3-hyperboloid

---

## Friedmann–Lemaître equations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Eliminating $ \Lambda $, and using conservation of mass and energy, we can derive:

- $$\mathop{ \rho }\limits^{ \cdot }=-3H( \rho +3p)$$

- Further, we can simplify the equations by scaling the mass density and pressure to include all of the constants:

- $$\begin{matrix}
{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=\frac{8 \pi G}{3} \rho -\frac{k{c}^{2}}{{R}^{2}} \\
\mathop{H}\limits^{ \cdot }+{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=-\frac{4 \pi G}{3}\left(  \rho +\frac{3p}{{c}^{2}} \right)
\end{matrix}$$

---

## Friedmann–Lemaître equations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Even more simplifications:
  - If we consider a perfect fluid, the pressure is proportional to the density: $p=w \rho $ for some constant $w$.
  - Space is flat ($k=0$)
  - Choose natural units ($c=1$)

- $$\begin{matrix}
{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=\frac{8 \pi G}{3} \rho  \\
\mathop{H}\limits^{ \cdot }+{H}^{2} & ={\left( \frac{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}{R} \right)}^{2}=-\frac{4 \pi G}{3}\left( 1+3w \right) \rho 
\end{matrix}$$

- This is homework problem 4!
  - Solve it both analytically and numerically.

## Celestial dynamics

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- 3-body ODE:

- $$\begin{aligned}
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{1}=-G{m}_{2}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{3}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}{|}^{3}} \\
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{2}=-G{m}_{1}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{3}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}{|}^{3}} \\
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{3}=-G{m}_{1}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{2}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}{|}^{3}}
\end{aligned}$$

- 9 degrees of freedom (3 bodies * 3 dimension).
- 7 independent conserved quantities (energy, linear momentum, angular momentum).
- Underconstrained problem: cannot solve exactly, except in special cases.
  - ... so we solve it numerically.

- Repeat from lectures on ODEs

## 2D 3-body problem

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Approximately solvable problem: 3-body motion, with:
  - Movement constrained to be co-planar (i.e. confined to x-y plane). Note, in general this is not stable (planets will deviate in z direction).
  - $${m}_{3}=0$$

- $$\begin{aligned}
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{1}=-G{m}_{2}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{3}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}{|}^{3}} \\
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{2}=-G{m}_{1}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{3}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{2}-{\mathbf{r}}_{3}{|}^{3}} \\
{\mathop{\mathbf{r}}\limits^{ \cdot  \cdot }}_{3}=-G{m}_{1}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{1}{|}^{3}}-G{m}_{2}\frac{{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}}{|{\mathbf{r}}_{3}-{\mathbf{r}}_{2}{|}^{3}}
\end{aligned}$$

- $${\mathbf{r}}_{i}=({x}_{i},{y}_{i})$$

- Repeat from lectures on ODEs

---

## 2D 3-body problem: effective potential

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Ignoring the Coriolis force for now, we can define an effective potential for this force.
  - Recall: orbiting in the Lennard–Jones potential, from the calculus lectures.

- $$V({x}^{′},{y}^{′})=-\frac{1- \alpha }{\sqrt{({x}^{′}- \alpha {)}^{2}+{y}^{′2}}}-\frac{ \alpha }{\sqrt{({x}^{′}+1- \alpha {)}^{2}+{y}^{′2}}}-\frac{{x}^{′2}+{y}^{′2}}{2}$$

- This potential has 5 extrema:
  - 2 maxima (L4, L5)
  - 3 saddle points (L1, L2, L3)
- These are the famous Lagrange points.
  - [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_point) is definitely worth a read :)

![File-Lagrange_points2.png](../assets/7.0_advdiffeq/File-Lagrange_points2.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}

- Lagrange points

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $N$-body problems are common in astrophysics:

  - Solar system with asteroid belt ($N \sim {10}^{5}$)
  - Star clusters ($N \sim {10}^{6}$)
  - Galaxies, dark matter halos
  - Galaxy clusters, large scale structure

  - Some problems in electrostatics, e.g. proteins and cellular assembly
  - Statistics/machine learning
  - Vortex methods in computation fluid dynamics

## $N$-body simulations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Onto computational aspects!
- Key problem: the long-range interaction.
- Let's say we have a uniform density of particles.
- Consider the effect on one particle from other particles in the shell $(r,r+ \delta r)$:
  - Force is $F \sim 1/{r}^{2}$
  - Number of particles $dN \sim 4 \pi {r}^{2} \delta r$
  - $$FdN \sim 4 \pi  \delta r$$
- Thus, the "total effect" is independent of $r$!
  - Cannot truncate the computation :(

![page39image19792.png](../assets/7.0_advdiffeq/page39image19792.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}

- Distribution of particles in N body problem

## $N$-body simulations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Code uses a “predictor-corrector” algorithm:
  - Step 1: predict position and velocity at next time step
    - (i.e. evolve system as a trial step, to be revised in a bit)
  - Step 2: computes acceleration and jerk at those predicted points using Taylor series

- $$\begin{matrix}
{\vec{r}}_{p} & =\vec{r}+\vec{v} \delta t+\frac{1}{2}\vec{a} \delta {t}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\vec{J} \delta {t}^{3} \\
{\vec{v}}_{p} & =\vec{v}+\vec{a} \delta t+\frac{1}{2}\vec{J} \delta {t}^{2}
\end{matrix}$$

- $$\begin{matrix}
\vec{k} &  \equiv \frac{1}{2}{\vec{a}}^{′′} \delta {t}^{2}=2(\vec{a}-{\vec{a}}_{p})+ \delta t(\vec{J}-{\vec{J}}_{p}) \\
\vec{l} &  \equiv \frac{1}{2}{\vec{a}}^{′′′} \delta {t}^{3}=-3(\vec{a}-{\vec{a}}_{p})- \delta t(2\vec{J}-{\vec{J}}_{p})
\end{matrix}$$

---

## $N$-body simulations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Code uses a “predictor-corrector” algorithm:
  - Step 3: use $\vec{k}$ and $\vec{l}$ to correct the trial ${\vec{r}}_{p}$ and ${\vec{v}}_{p}$:
- Additionally, the code is adaptive: time step is adjusted based on "least collision time," the smallest time between interactions of two objects
  - Intuition: if two particles happen to be close, it's more important, so reduce the time step.
  - Similar to adaptive RK4(5) algorithm.

- $$\begin{matrix}
{\vec{r}}_{c} & ={\vec{r}}_{p}+\left( \frac{1}{12}\vec{k}+\frac{1}{20}\vec{l} \right) \delta {t}^{2} \\
{\vec{v}}_{c} & ={\vec{v}}_{p}+\left( \frac{1}{3}\vec{k}+\frac{1}{4}\vec{l} \right) \delta t
\end{matrix}$$

## $N$-body simulations

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- The full $N$-body problem is $O({N}^{2})$ :( How do we improve?
- Particle mesh:
  - Create a 3D lattice; approximate forces from lattice cells, rather than each particle.
  - Good for uniform configurations.
  - $O(Mlog(M))$, where $M=$#(grid points)
- Trees:
  - Partition space into hierarchy of cubes of different sizes: "octree" algorithm.
  - Compute particle-particle interactions for close interactions
  - Compute cell-cell (or particle-cell) interactions for far interactions
  - $O(Nlog(N))$, $N=$#(particles)

## $N$-body simulations

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- How do we improve the computational complexity?
- Fast multipole methods
  - Expands Green's function in a multipole
  - $O(N)$, $N=$#(particles)
- Fluid dynamics approximations
  - Approximate by PDEs, not individual particles
  - Obviously, only applicable for specific (fluid) problems.

## Asteroid belt simulation

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- One last exercise for $N$-body problem: simulating the asteroid belt.
  - Notebooks based on [https://github.com/alvinng4/](https://github.com/alvinng4/)
- Some of you have probably wondered: how do I add software to the Docker environment?
  - To some extent... you don't!
  - Recall that most folders in the container are transient, and are deleted when you stop the container.
  - So, if you apt install emacs, it will be installed under e.g. /usr/bin, and deleted when you close the container!
  - Same goes for pip.
- Workaround: you can do local installations in persistent folders (e.g. mounted CompPhys folder, or a Docker volume).

## A warning about Docker

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- In principle, you can pip install grav_sim inside our Docker container
  - Remember, aside from mounted folders, everything in the container is transient, and will vanish when you stop the container!
  - If nothing else, this is a good demonstration of what Docker is not good at. For installing a python package, using conda or virtualenv is a better idea.
- If you want to get it working via Docker, you can tell pip to install in a specific location (the mounted CompPhys folder):

- # Start outside container
- cd CompPhys
- git clone git@github.com:DryRun/grav_sim.git
- mkdir .local/lib/python3.12/site-packages
- chmod -R a+w grav_sim
- chmod -R a+w .local
- ./runDocker.sh ubsuny/compphys:latest # or runDocker_wfix.sh
- # Inside container now
- export CMAKE_ARGS="-DUSE_HDF5=ON" # Compile w/HDF5 libraries
- export PYTHONPATH=/home/compphys/CompPhys/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages
- python -m pip install --target CompPhys/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages CompPhys/grav_sim

## Virtual environments

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- A simpler way: python virtual environments or conda.
  - The venv module supports creating lightweight “virtual environments”, each with their own independent set of Python packages installed in their [site](https://docs.python.org/3/library/site.html#module-site) directories. A virtual environment is created on top of an existing Python installation, known as the virtual environment’s “base” Python, and by default is isolated from the packages in the base environment, so that only those explicitly installed in the virtual environment are available.
  - Conda package manager works similarly (more extensive, some licensing concerns)
  - Note: venv and conda are not compatible! Choose one.
- Virtual environments are a simple way to isolate a project's code, which is ~always a good idea.
  - Uses environment variables like PYTHONPATH to control where python looks for modules
- Check out [https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)
- Demo grav_sim installation and [packaging](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/)

- You might want to use this for your project!

## Kirkwood gaps

- original version:: : Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- [Kirkwood gaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkwood_gap) are gaps in the distribution of asteroids in particular orbits (i.e., specific semi-major axes or orbital periods)
- Originate from orbital resonances with planets, particularly Jupiter
  - E.g. gap near semi-major axis = 2.50 AU, period = 3.95 years
  - This correspond to a 3:1 resonance with Jupiter
  - Resonance induces chaotic motion, disrupting orbits
